tabs.title: A Festival Changes
tabs.description: Compare the new cup system with last year.

tabs.title: Planning an Event
tabs.description: Transfer the ideas to a school activity.

questions.q: Why did the festival organisers decide to change their cup system?
choices: Visitors did not want any water.
The music finished too early.
Too many plastic cups were left after concerts.
The town had no grass left.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies litter after concerts as the problem.

questions.q: What did the organisers do to help people find water without buying many bottles?
choices: They provided free places where people could get water.
They closed all food stalls.
They asked visitors to bring drinks only from home.
They stopped selling festival tickets.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two says visitors had access to free water stations and could bring bottles.

questions.q: Why might children collect cups left on the ground?
choices: They wanted to stop the concerts.
They could get the deposits for returned cups.
They were paid to wash every cup.
They were looking for their school bags.
questions.explanation: Children could collect the return money as pocket money.

questions.q: How did clear signs and another return desk address visitors' worries?
choices: They kept the grass dry.
They made the cups smaller.
They stopped people bringing bottles.
They made the new system easier to use and reduced waiting.
questions.explanation: The organisers responded to concerns about queues with signs and a second desk.

questions.q: Why should the organisers not say they have solved all the rubbish problems?
choices: The festival no longer has any visitors.
The return system did not allow drinking water.
They still had food wrappers and other waste to collect.
Every reusable cup disappeared.
questions.explanation: The account says the new system was helpful but not perfect.

questions.q: What does the change in rubbish-bag numbers suggest?
choices: The festival produced less collected litter on Saturday night.
The cleaning team worked more hours.
Every item of rubbish was recycled.
The number of visitors fell by half.
questions.explanation: The cleaners filled twenty-six bags instead of forty the previous year.

questions.q: A school wants to reduce rubbish after lunch. Which next step fits the festival's plan?
choices: Stop students using all bins.
Make students buy a new cup daily.
Move all rubbish to the playground.
Ask food sellers to use less packaging too.
questions.explanation: The organisers plan to tackle food packaging because many wrappers remain.

questions.q: Why could a refundable deposit encourage people to return an item?
choices: The item becomes free to manufacture.
People receive their money again when they bring it back.
Visitors can avoid paying for tickets.
It makes food packaging disappear.
questions.explanation: The two-euro deposit is returned when a cup is handed back.

questions.q: A volunteer says, 'Some cups were lost, so the new system was a failure.' What is a fairer response?
choices: It helped reduce litter although some problems remained.
The system made the grass much dirtier.
No visitor managed to find the water stations.
All the old cups were reused.
questions.explanation: The article reports improvement alongside missing cups and remaining litter.

questions.q: What is the best reason to count rubbish bags next year as well?
choices: To decide which singer should perform.
To give children more pocket money.
To see whether the changes continue to make a difference.
To make the cups heavier.
questions.explanation: Counting bags allows the organisers to compare the amount of waste after further changes.
